claims.text: An integrated approach combining ab initio datasets with machine-learning-accelerated molecular dynamics can accurately and efficiently predict melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across high-entropy alloys.
Machine-learning potentials trained on DFT data can be used with accelerated molecular dynamics to simulate melting.
The extent of short-range order in the solid and liquid states mediates changes in thermodynamic properties across melting.
Machine-learning potentials can capture the relevant multi-element interactions in high-entropy alloys.
Capturing multi-element interactions enables efficient exploration of the disordered liquid state.
The proposed potentials preserve the essential physics of atomic diffusion.
The proposed potentials preserve the essential physics of local volume fluctuations.
The proposed potentials preserve the essential physics of entropic contributions.
The simulation can resolve melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase properties at lower cost than full ab initio molecular dynamics.
Predicted melting temperatures, latent heats, fusion entropies, and volume changes will agree with experiment within approximately 10% on average.
The method will reduce computational time by orders of magnitude relative to full ab initio simulations.
Standard ab initio molecular dynamics is accurate for the relevant melting and thermodynamic calculations.
Standard ab initio molecular dynamics is computationally prohibitive for broad exploration of high-entropy-alloy composition space.
Extremely complex local chemical order may limit the method's applicability.
Significant electronic-correlation effects may limit the method's applicability.
Insufficient training-set coverage of relevant configurations, especially high-temperature liquid configurations, may reduce prediction reliability.
Prediction errors may range from 5% to 15% depending on the alloy system.
Deviation exceeding 15% for a majority of tested high-entropy alloys is specified as the result that would falsify the approach.
